title: Medicare Spending, the Physician Workforce, and Beneficiaries' Quality of Care
research_question: Does higher Medicare spending per beneficiary translate into better quality of care for the elderly? More broadly, what role does the composition of the local physician workforce — particularly the balance between general practitioners and specialists — play in shaping both spending levels and the use of effective, high-quality care?
data_description: The study uses U.S. state-level data on Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries. Twenty-four quality-of-care measures for 2000–01 (and a subset of four available in 1995 and 1999) come from the Medicare Quality Improvement Organization, covering treatments for acute myocardial infarction, breast cancer, diabetes, heart failure, pneumonia, and stroke (e.g., beta-blockers at discharge, mammography, HbA1c testing, eye exams). Medicare reimbursement per beneficiary, end-of-life utilization (hospital days and ICU admissions in the last six months of life), AMI discharges, and mortality come from the Dartmouth Atlas Medicare claims data, adjusted for inflation, state cost of living, and beneficiary age/sex/race. Patient satisfaction and HMO penetration come from the 1992–1995 Medicare Current Beneficiary Survey. Workforce counts (specialists, general practitioners, registered nurses) come from the 2003 Area Resource File, scaled by 2000 Census population.
institutional_context: Medicare spending per beneficiary varies substantially across U.S. states, as does the quality of care that elderly beneficiaries receive — for example, beta-blocker administration after heart attacks ranged from 50 percent in Alabama to 86 percent in New Hampshire in 2000. With Medicare facing mounting fiscal pressures and policymakers debating reforms, it is important to understand whether spending more produces better care. States also differ markedly in the composition of their physician workforce, with some areas dominated by primary-care generalists and others by specialists, and in their reliance on intensive end-of-life hospital and ICU care. These geographic differences in resource allocation, practice style, and provider mix create the setting in which the relationship between cost, workforce composition, and the delivery of inexpensive but highly effective preventive and acute-care services can be assessed.
